authored_against: Grade 5 science, elementary band. Keys state established science at this grade band; they are not extracted from the source, which states only a focus and generic objectives.

relationships: A phenomenon is something that happens in the world and can be observed; science starts from phenomena rather than from definitions.
An observation reports what happened; an explanation says why, and the two are recorded separately.
A phenomenon worth investigating usually contains something that does not fit what the observer expected.
accepted_alternative_framings: Qualitative and quantitative observations are both observations; neither is required to be present.
disqualifying_errors: Recording an explanation in the observation column.
Treating a personal opinion about a phenomenon as data.
Claiming a phenomenon must be unusual or dramatic to be worth investigating.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal uncertainty analysis and instrument calibration are later grades.

relationships: A testable question names what will be changed or compared and what will be observed or measured.
A question is testable only if some possible result would count against it.
Questions of value or preference are not settled by observation, however carefully they are asked.
accepted_alternative_framings: Comparison, cause, and 'what happens if' forms are all testable question types.
disqualifying_errors: Calling a question testable when no observation could disconfirm it.
Framing a preference as a testable question.
Claiming a question must begin with 'why' to be scientific.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal hypothesis statements and named variables are later work.

relationships: A model represents a system in order to explain or predict its behaviour.
Every model simplifies; the simplification is a stated limitation, not a defect to conceal.
A model is tested by whether its predictions match observation, not by how detailed it looks.
accepted_alternative_framings: Diagrams, physical builds, flow charts, and written descriptions are all legitimate models here.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a model must resemble the real thing to be useful.
Claiming a model has no limitations.
Judging a model on presentation rather than on what it predicts or explains.
topics.out_of_scope: Mathematical and computational models are Grade 7 and later work.

fixed_facts: A fair test changes one variable and holds the others constant.
relationships: A fair test changes one thing on purpose and holds constant everything else that could affect the result.
If two conditions change together, the result cannot be attributed to either.
Repeating trials shows whether a result is reproducible; a single trial cannot.
disqualifying_errors: Calling a test fair when more than one condition changed.
Treating a single trial as proof of a result.
Discarding a trial because it disagreed with the others, without saying so and why.
topics.out_of_scope: Control groups by name, randomisation, and sample-size reasoning are later work.

fixed_facts: A measurement is incomplete without its unit.
relationships: A measurement has a number and a unit, and comparisons require the same unit.
A data table with labelled columns, units in the headings, and one row per trial can be read by someone who was not present.
Repeated measurements of the same quantity vary a little; that variation is information about the method.
accepted_alternative_framings: Metric or customary units are both acceptable if used consistently within a comparison.
disqualifying_errors: Recording values with no units.
Adjusting a recorded value so it fits the expected pattern.
Claiming that more decimal places always means a more accurate measurement.
topics.out_of_scope: Significant figures and formal uncertainty ranges are Grade 7 and later work.

relationships: Criteria state what a successful solution must achieve; constraints state the limits it must respect, including materials, cost, time, and safety.
Criteria and constraints are set before solutions are generated, so all options are judged the same way.
A solution that violates a constraint has not solved the problem, however well it scores on the criteria.
disqualifying_errors: Treating criteria and constraints as interchangeable.
Declaring a solution best without stating the criteria.
Revising the criteria after testing so a preferred solution wins.
topics.out_of_scope: Weighted decision matrices and formal optimisation are later work.

fixed_facts: Matter is made of particles too small to be seen.
relationships: All matter is made of particles that are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
Because matter is made of particles, a substance can be present even when it cannot be seen, as air is.
The particle model explains why matter that seems to disappear, such as evaporating water or dissolving sugar, has not stopped existing.
accepted_alternative_framings: Calling them particles, or atoms and molecules, are both acceptable at this grade; the source's own wording is not required.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a gas is not matter because it cannot be seen.
Claiming dissolved or evaporated material has ceased to exist.
Claiming particles can be seen directly with a hand lens or school microscope.
topics.out_of_scope: Atomic structure, the periodic table, and molecular formulas are Grade 7 and later work.

relationships: Materials can be described by observable properties such as colour, hardness, texture, flexibility, magnetic attraction, conductivity, solubility, and whether they float in water.
Some properties do not depend on how much of the material there is, and those are the useful ones for identifying it.
A single property rarely identifies a material; several together do much better.
disqualifying_errors: Identifying a material from colour alone.
Treating the amount of a sample as a property of the material.
Claiming two materials must be the same because they share one property.
topics.out_of_scope: The intensive-extensive distinction by name, and density as a calculated quantity, are Grade 7 and later work.

fixed_facts: Mass and volume are different quantities and are measured in different units.
relationships: Mass is how much matter an object contains; volume is how much space it takes up.
Two objects of the same volume can have different masses, and two objects of the same mass can have different volumes.
Mass is measured with a balance and volume by measuring dimensions or by displacement.
accepted_alternative_framings: Weight and mass are distinguished in later grades; at this grade a learner who uses them interchangeably in everyday contexts is not wrong unless the lesson turns on the distinction.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a larger object always has more mass.
Reporting a volume in mass units, or a mass in volume units.
Claiming mass changes when an object changes shape.
topics.out_of_scope: Density as mass divided by volume, and the mass-weight distinction as a graded idea, are Grade 7 and later work.

relationships: A material is identified by testing several properties and comparing the results with known materials.
The more properties that match, the stronger the identification.
An identification is a conclusion supported by evidence, and it can be revised if a further test disagrees.
disqualifying_errors: Declaring an identification certain on the strength of one property.
Ignoring a test result that disagrees with the preferred identification.
Claiming an unknown must be one of the samples offered when none of the properties match.
topics.out_of_scope: Chemical tests, flame tests, and analytical identification are later work.

fixed_facts: In a mixture, the substances keep their own properties and can in principle be separated.
relationships: A mixture contains two or more substances that keep their own properties.
Mixtures can be separated by physical means such as filtering, sieving, evaporating, or using a magnet, because the substances have not been changed.
A substance that has dissolved is still present in the mixture, and evaporating the liquid recovers it.
accepted_alternative_framings: Solutions are mixtures; a learner who calls dissolved sugar in water a mixture or a solution is correct either way.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming dissolving destroys the dissolved substance.
Claiming a mixture cannot be separated because it looks uniform.
Claiming any combination of substances is a new substance.
topics.out_of_scope: Solubility curves, concentration units, and the compound-versus-mixture distinction in chemical terms are Grade 7 and later work.

relationships: A measuring tool can only resolve differences down to its smallest division; smaller differences than that are not measured, they are guessed.
Repeating a measurement and getting similar values shows the method is reproducible.
Precision is about how closely repeated measurements agree; being close together is not the same as being right.
disqualifying_errors: Reporting a measurement to more places than the tool can resolve.
Claiming precise measurements must be accurate.
Discarding a value that disagrees, without recording that it was discarded and why.
topics.out_of_scope: Significant figures, standard deviation, and formal uncertainty are Grade 7 and later work.

fixed_facts: In a physical change no new substance is formed.
relationships: A physical change alters the form, state, or appearance of a substance without producing a new substance.
Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, dissolving, breaking, and bending are physical changes.
The total mass does not change during a physical change, even when the material seems to disappear.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming that melting or boiling turns a substance into a different substance.
Claiming mass is lost when a liquid evaporates from an open container, rather than that the vapour has left the container.
Claiming a change is physical because it can be reversed and chemical because it cannot; reversibility is a clue, not the definition.
topics.out_of_scope: Phase-change energy, latent heat, and particle-level state diagrams are Grade 7 and later work.

relationships: Mixing two substances sometimes produces a mixture and sometimes produces new substances.
Which of the two happened is decided by evidence, not by whether the result looks different.
When only a mixture forms, the original substances are still there and can in principle be separated.
disqualifying_errors: Concluding a new substance formed only because the appearance changed.
Claiming any two substances mixed together always react.
Claiming a mixture cannot be separated once it has been stirred.
topics.out_of_scope: Reaction equations, reactants and products by name, and reaction types are Grade 7 and later work.

fixed_facts: Evidence of a chemical change includes gas production, a temperature change not caused by heating or cooling from outside, a colour change, a precipitate forming, light being given off, and an odour appearing.
relationships: A chemical change produces one or more new substances with different properties.
Signs that suggest a chemical change include gas bubbles, an unexpected temperature change, colour change, a solid forming from clear liquids, light, and a new smell.
Any single sign can have another explanation, so several lines of evidence make the conclusion stronger.
accepted_alternative_framings: Chemical change and chemical reaction are the same idea at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Treating bubbling alone as proof of a chemical change, when boiling and dissolved gas escaping also bubble.
Claiming a colour change always means a chemical change.
Claiming a chemical change destroys matter.
topics.out_of_scope: Balancing equations, reaction energetics, and reaction rate are Grade 7 and later work.

fixed_facts: In any physical or chemical change, the total mass of the substances is the same before and after.
relationships: The total mass of matter is the same before and after a change, whether physical or chemical.
Mass that appears to be lost has usually left the container as a gas, and mass that appears to be gained has usually entered it from the air.
Testing conservation of mass requires a closed system, or an accounting of everything that entered or left.
accepted_alternative_framings: Saying matter is conserved, or that atoms are neither created nor destroyed, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming mass is destroyed when a substance burns or dissolves.
Claiming mass is created when a solid forms from two solutions.
Concluding mass was not conserved from an open-container measurement without accounting for what entered or left.
topics.out_of_scope: Stoichiometry, the mole, and mass-energy equivalence are High School work.

relationships: A closed system does not exchange matter with its surroundings; an open system does.
Conservation of mass is directly observable in a closed system, and in an open one only if what crosses the boundary is accounted for.
Defining the boundary of the system is part of the investigation, not a detail.
disqualifying_errors: Treating an open container as a closed system.
Claiming conservation of mass fails because an open system lost mass.
Reporting a system without saying where its boundary was drawn.
topics.out_of_scope: Isolated systems and energy exchange across boundaries are later work.

relationships: A claim about a change is supported by measurements taken before and after under the same conditions.
A difference smaller than the measuring tool can resolve is not evidence of a change.
Every reported value states its unit and how it was obtained.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a change from a difference smaller than the tool can resolve.
Comparing before and after measurements taken with different tools or methods, without saying so.
Reporting a measurement without a unit.
topics.out_of_scope: Uncertainty propagation and statistical tests are later work.

fixed_facts: The energy in almost all food can be traced back to energy from the Sun.
relationships: Plants capture energy from sunlight and use it to make their own food.
The energy in the food animals eat can be traced back to the Sun through the plants at the base of the food chain.
The Sun is the source of the energy that drives most processes at Earth's surface, including weather and the water cycle.
accepted_alternative_framings: Saying plants make food using light energy, or that they carry out photosynthesis, are both correct here.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming plants take in food from the soil rather than making it.
Claiming animals get their energy directly from sunlight.
Claiming energy is created inside an organism.
topics.out_of_scope: The chemistry of photosynthesis and ATP are Grade 7 and High School work.

relationships: Food provides organisms with both energy and the materials their bodies are built from.
The energy an animal uses for motion, growth, warmth, and repair comes from its food.
Food energy that is not used immediately is stored, not destroyed.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming animals make their own food inside their bodies.
Claiming food supplies energy but not the materials for growth.
Claiming unused food energy simply disappears.
topics.out_of_scope: Cellular respiration as a chemical process, and calorie accounting, are Grade 7 and High School work.

fixed_facts: Energy moves through a food web in one direction, from producers to consumers to decomposers.
relationships: Energy enters an ecosystem through producers and passes to consumers when they eat.
At every transfer most of the energy is released to the surroundings, mainly as warmth, so less is available at each successive level.
Arrows in a food web point in the direction the energy and matter travel, that is, from the organism eaten to the organism eating it.
accepted_alternative_framings: Food chain and food web are both correct representations; a web shows more of the connections.
disqualifying_errors: Drawing food-web arrows pointing from the eater to the eaten.
Claiming energy cycles round a food web the way matter does.
Claiming all the energy at one level passes to the next.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative trophic efficiency figures and energy pyramids with numbers are Grade 7 and High School work.

fixed_facts: The gravitational force Earth exerts on objects is directed toward Earth's centre, which is what 'down' means.
relationships: Earth pulls objects toward its centre; that pull is what is called gravity, and it is why unsupported objects fall.
The direction called 'down' is toward Earth's centre, and it is different at different places on the globe.
Gravity acts on an object whether it is moving or at rest, and whether or not it is touching anything.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming gravity acts only on falling objects and not on ones sitting still.
Claiming there is no gravity in space, or that astronauts float because gravity has stopped.
Claiming heavier objects always fall noticeably faster than lighter ones through air, without reference to air resistance.
topics.out_of_scope: Newton's law of gravitation, weight as a calculated force, and orbital mechanics are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: Motion is described relative to something else, so the reference point is stated.
Observing motion means recording position at stated times, not only whether something moved.
Patterns in recorded motion support predictions about motion under the same conditions.
disqualifying_errors: Describing motion with no reference point stated.
Reporting that an object moved without saying over what time or distance.
Predicting motion for conditions the observations never covered.
topics.out_of_scope: Velocity as a vector, acceleration, and motion graphs are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: A causal claim names what was changed and what changed as a result.
Two things varying together is not sufficient evidence that one causes the other.
Evidence for causation comes from changing one factor while holding others constant, and observing what follows.
disqualifying_errors: Inferring cause from co-occurrence alone.
Reversing cause and effect with no evidence about order.
Naming an effect with no proposed cause and calling it an explanation.
topics.out_of_scope: Confounding variables by name and correlation coefficients are later work.

fixed_facts: Plants need light, water, air, and a suitable temperature to grow; soil supplies minerals and support, not food.
relationships: Plants need light, water, air, and suitable temperature in order to grow.
Soil provides water, dissolved minerals, and physical support; it does not supply the plant's food.
Removing any one of a plant's needs limits its growth, however plentiful the others are.
accepted_alternative_framings: Saying plants need carbon dioxide, or that they need air, are both correct at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming plants take in food from the soil.
Claiming soil is the main source of the material a plant's body is built from.
Claiming a plant can grow indefinitely with water alone.
topics.out_of_scope: The photosynthesis equation and mineral nutrition detail are Grade 7 and High School work.

topics.focus: air and water as matter sources
fixed_facts: Most of the material a plant's body is built from comes from air and water, not from soil.
relationships: The material that makes up a plant comes chiefly from air and water, not from the soil it grows in.
The carbon in a plant's body comes from carbon dioxide taken in from the air.
Soil loses very little mass as a plant growing in it gains a great deal, which is the evidence for this.
accepted_alternative_framings: Saying the plant's mass comes from air and water, or that carbon comes from carbon dioxide and hydrogen and oxygen from water, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a plant's mass comes mainly from the soil.
Claiming a plant gains mass from fertiliser as its principal building material.
Claiming air contributes nothing to a plant's body because it cannot be seen.
topics.out_of_scope: The full photosynthesis equation and carbon fixation chemistry are High School work.

fixed_facts: Producers make their own food; consumers eat other organisms; decomposers break down dead material and wastes.
relationships: Producers make their own food, usually using light; consumers get food by eating other organisms; decomposers break down dead organisms and wastes.
Decomposers return matter from dead organisms to the soil, water, and air, where producers can use it again.
Without decomposers, matter would stay locked in dead material and the cycle would stop.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming fungi and bacteria as decomposers, or describing detritivores among them, are both acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Classifying a plant as a consumer because it takes in water and minerals.
Claiming decomposers are harmful organisms with no role in the ecosystem.
Claiming dead material simply disappears without decomposers acting on it.
topics.out_of_scope: Chemoautotrophs, trophic-level arithmetic, and nutrient-cycle chemistry are later work.

relationships: A food web shows the feeding relationships in an ecosystem, with arrows pointing from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it.
Most organisms appear in more than one chain within a web, which is why a web represents an ecosystem better than a single chain.
Changing the number of one organism affects others in the web, sometimes several steps away.
disqualifying_errors: Drawing arrows from predator to prey.
Claiming removing one organism affects only the one directly above it.
Claiming a food web shows energy returning from consumers to producers.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative population modelling and trophic cascades by name are later work.

fixed_facts: Matter cycles among organisms and the environment; energy flows through and does not cycle.
relationships: Matter cycles repeatedly between organisms and the air, water, and soil around them.
The same atoms are used over and over by different organisms across time.
Energy, unlike matter, flows through an ecosystem in one direction and is not recycled.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming energy cycles through an ecosystem the way matter does.
Claiming matter is used up and lost from the ecosystem.
Claiming new matter is created by organisms as they grow.
topics.out_of_scope: Named biogeochemical cycles with reservoirs and fluxes are Grade 7 and High School work.

relationships: Organisms in an ecosystem depend on one another and on the non-living parts of their environment.
A change to one part of an ecosystem can affect parts that are not directly connected to it.
Interdependence means an ecosystem's behaviour cannot be predicted by looking at one organism alone.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming each organism in an ecosystem is independent of the others.
Claiming the non-living parts of an environment are not part of the ecosystem.
Predicting the effect of a change by considering only the directly connected organism.
topics.out_of_scope: Keystone species, resilience metrics, and quantitative community ecology are later work.

fixed_facts: Earth's major systems are the geosphere, the hydrosphere, the atmosphere, and the biosphere.
relationships: Earth's major systems are the geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere, and they interact continuously.
Nearly every Earth process involves more than one of these systems at once.
The four-system division is a model for thinking about Earth, not a set of physically separate compartments.
accepted_alternative_framings: Including the cryosphere as part of the hydrosphere, or naming it separately, are both acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the systems operate independently of one another.
Placing living things outside Earth's systems.
Claiming the boundaries between the systems are sharp physical divisions.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative system fluxes and feedback analysis are High School work.

fixed_facts: About 97 per cent of Earth's water is salt water in the ocean.
Of the small fresh-water fraction, most is frozen in glaciers and ice caps, and only a small part is liquid fresh water available at the surface or underground.
relationships: Almost all of Earth's water is salt water in the ocean; fresh water is a small fraction of the total.
Most fresh water is frozen in glaciers and ice sheets rather than available as liquid.
Liquid fresh water is unevenly distributed across Earth, which is why availability differs so much between regions.
accepted_alternative_framings: Approximate figures such as 'about 97 per cent' or 'nearly all' are both acceptable; exact percentages are not required.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming most of Earth's water is fresh.
Claiming most fresh water is in lakes and rivers.
Claiming fresh water is evenly available everywhere on Earth.
topics.out_of_scope: Reservoir residence times and quantitative water budgets are High School work.

relationships: Water at the surface collects in streams, rivers, lakes, and wetlands, and water underground fills spaces between soil particles and cracks in rock.
Surface water and groundwater are connected: water moves between them, so what happens to one affects the other.
Water moves downhill at the surface and moves through the ground much more slowly than it moves in a river.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing groundwater as filling pore spaces, or as being held in an aquifer, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming groundwater flows in underground rivers everywhere beneath the surface.
Claiming surface water and groundwater are separate supplies that never mix.
Claiming pollution at the surface cannot reach groundwater.
topics.out_of_scope: Hydraulic conductivity, aquifer modelling, and recharge rates are High School work.

relationships: An interaction between Earth's systems is described by naming both systems and what passes between them.
One event usually involves several interactions at once, such as a storm moving water from atmosphere to geosphere and biosphere.
Interactions can change a system enough to change how it interacts next, which is why Earth systems do not stay in a fixed state.
disqualifying_errors: Naming an interaction without saying what moves between the systems.
Claiming an interaction goes only one way when it goes both.
Claiming a change in one system leaves all the others unaffected.
topics.out_of_scope: Named feedback loops and quantitative coupling are High School work.

relationships: Maps and data tables show where Earth's water, land, and features are, and patterns in them are evidence about processes.
A map needs a key, a scale, and a stated source before its patterns can be relied on.
Data shown on a map is still data: it has a date, a source, and limits on what it covers.
disqualifying_errors: Reading distances or quantities from a map with no scale or key.
Treating an undated map as showing current conditions.
Claiming a pattern on a map explains itself without any proposed process.
topics.out_of_scope: Projection distortion and geographic information systems are later work.

relationships: The amount and timing of water available differ from region to region because of climate, landforms, and the geology beneath.
Regions with plenty of surface water can still face shortage if the water is polluted, seasonal, or shared between many users.
A region's water pattern is described over years, not from a single measurement.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a region near a large lake or river cannot have a water problem.
Describing a region's water pattern from one season's data.
Claiming water availability depends on rainfall alone.
topics.out_of_scope: Water-budget calculation and drought indices are later work.

fixed_facts: Stars differ in how bright they actually are and in how far away they are, and both affect how bright they look from Earth.
relationships: How bright a star looks from Earth depends on how much light it actually gives out and on how far away it is.
A star that looks dim may be very bright but far away; a star that looks bright may be modest but close.
Distance cannot be read off apparent brightness alone.
accepted_alternative_framings: Apparent and actual brightness, or apparent and absolute brightness, are both acceptable namings.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the brightest-looking star must be the closest.
Claiming all stars give out the same amount of light.
Claiming a star's apparent brightness alone establishes its distance.
topics.out_of_scope: The inverse-square law, magnitude scales, and parallax measurement are High School work.

fixed_facts: The Sun is a star, and it appears larger and brighter than other stars because it is far closer to Earth.
relationships: The Sun is an ordinary star; it looks different from the others only because it is enormously closer.
Other stars are suns too, at distances so great that they appear as points of light.
The Sun's apparent size and brightness are consequences of its distance, not of it being a different kind of object.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the Sun is not a star.
Claiming the Sun is the largest or brightest star that exists.
Claiming other stars are small because they look small.
topics.out_of_scope: Stellar classification, fusion, and stellar life cycles are High School work.

fixed_facts: Day and night are caused by Earth rotating on its axis, not by the Sun moving around Earth.
relationships: Earth's rotation on its axis causes the daily cycle of day and night and the apparent movement of the Sun across the sky.
A shadow is longest when the Sun is lowest in the sky and shortest when it is highest, so shadows change in a repeating daily pattern.
A shadow points away from the light source, so shadow direction changes through the day as the Sun's apparent position changes.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the Sun orbits Earth each day.
Claiming shadows are longest at midday.
Claiming day and night are caused by Earth's orbit around the Sun rather than by its rotation.
topics.out_of_scope: Solar altitude calculations, solar time, and the analemma are later work.

fixed_facts: Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not by Earth's distance from the Sun.
relationships: The length of daylight and the Sun's height in the sky change through the year in a repeating pattern.
These seasonal patterns are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis as Earth orbits the Sun.
Because of the tilt, the Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time of year.
accepted_alternative_framings: Explaining the tilt effect as a change in the directness of sunlight, or as a change in day length, are both correct and usually both apply.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer.
Claiming both hemispheres have summer at the same time.
Claiming the tilt of Earth's axis changes direction through the year.
topics.out_of_scope: Solstice and equinox geometry in quantitative terms, and axial precession, are later work.

relationships: Patterns in the sky are found by recording observations over days, months, or a year, not from single observations.
The record states the date, time, and place of each observation, because all three affect what is seen.
A pattern found over one period supports predictions only for conditions the record actually covered.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a yearly pattern from a few days of observation.
Recording sky observations without date, time, and location.
Extending a pattern to a season or a latitude the record never covered.
topics.out_of_scope: Time-series analysis and formal periodicity tests are later work.

relationships: A scale model of the sky or the solar system cannot usually keep both sizes and distances to the same scale, because the distances are so much larger.
The model's limitation is stated alongside it, so nobody reads the wrong lesson from it.
A model is useful for the relationships it does represent, even when it distorts others.
disqualifying_errors: Reading planet sizes or distances off a classroom model as though they were to scale.
Claiming a model that distorts scale is simply wrong rather than limited.
Presenting a scale model without stating what it does not represent.
topics.out_of_scope: Astronomical units, light years, and logarithmic scaling are Grade 8 and High School work.

fixed_facts: Renewable resources are replenished on a human timescale; non-renewable resources are not.
relationships: People use Earth's resources for energy, food, water, materials, and shelter.
Renewable resources are replenished on a human timescale; non-renewable resources are used faster than they form.
A renewable resource can still be exhausted locally if it is used faster than it is replenished.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming renewable resources cannot be depleted.
Claiming fossil fuels are renewable because they are still forming somewhere.
Claiming resource use has no environmental effect if the resource is renewable.
topics.out_of_scope: Reserve estimation and resource economics are later work.

relationships: Waste and pollutants released into air, water, or land do not disappear; they move through Earth's systems.
A pollutant released in one place can affect a different place, because air and water carry it.
The effect of a pollutant depends on how much there is, how long it lasts, and what it reaches.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming waste disposed of out of sight has left the environment.
Claiming pollution affects only the place it was released.
Claiming any detectable amount of a substance is necessarily harmful, or that a small amount never is, without reference to the amount and the exposure.
topics.out_of_scope: Toxicology, dose-response, and pollutant transport modelling are later work.

relationships: Conservation strategies reduce use, reuse materials, recycle them, or protect a resource from damage.
A strategy's effect is judged by evidence of what changed, not by how popular or well-intentioned it is.
Reducing use generally has a larger effect than recycling the same material, because recycling itself takes energy and materials.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming recycling makes unlimited use sustainable.
Claiming a strategy works without any evidence of its effect.
Claiming a strategy that works in one setting must work everywhere.
topics.out_of_scope: Life-cycle assessment and quantitative footprint accounting are later work.

relationships: Environmental decisions involve trade-offs: a benefit for one group or one goal often comes with a cost to another.
Who bears the cost and who receives the benefit are part of the evidence, not a separate question.
A decision that ignores a trade-off has not removed it.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting a solution as having benefits and no costs.
Claiming everyone in a community is affected equally by a decision.
Treating a trade-off as settled by preference rather than by evidence about effects.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal cost-benefit analysis and policy frameworks are later work.

relationships: A decision is evidence-based when the evidence is named, its source is given, and the reasoning from evidence to decision is shown.
Evidence can constrain a decision without settling it, because decisions also involve values.
Evidence that argues against the preferred option is reported, not omitted.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting a decision as evidence-based with no evidence cited.
Omitting evidence that counts against the chosen option.
Claiming evidence alone determines what should be done.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal decision theory and stakeholder analysis are later work.

relationships: Criteria for an environmental solution state what it must achieve in terms that can be checked with evidence.
Constraints include cost, time, available materials, safety, and law.
Criteria are set before options are compared, and every option is judged against the same set.
disqualifying_errors: Writing a criterion that no evidence could ever check.
Comparing options against different criteria.
Changing the criteria after the comparison so a preferred option wins.
topics.out_of_scope: Weighted scoring and formal requirements analysis are later work.

relationships: A system is defined by its boundary, its parts, and the flows of matter and energy across that boundary.
A system's behaviour comes from the interactions between its parts, not from any one part alone.
Changing where the boundary is drawn changes what counts as inside the system and what counts as an input.
disqualifying_errors: Describing a system without stating its boundary.
Explaining a system's behaviour from one part in isolation.
Claiming a system model captures everything about the real system.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative system dynamics and feedback modelling are High School work.

relationships: A causal claim names the change made and the change that followed, and rules out the obvious alternatives.
Correlation is not causation; things can vary together because a third factor drives both.
In a system with many interacting parts, one effect can have several contributing causes.
disqualifying_errors: Inferring cause from things happening together.
Assuming an effect has exactly one cause.
Reversing cause and effect without evidence about which came first.
topics.out_of_scope: Confounding, controlled experimental design vocabulary, and statistics are later work.

fixed_facts: Matter cycles within a system; energy flows through it and is not recycled.
relationships: Matter cycles within and between systems, while energy flows through them in one direction.
Tracking matter and tracking energy are two different accounts of the same process, and both are needed.
Neither matter nor energy is created or destroyed within a system; both can only enter, leave, or change form.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming energy cycles the way matter does.
Claiming matter or energy is created or destroyed inside a system.
Treating an account of matter as though it also accounted for energy.
topics.out_of_scope: Entropy, the second law, and quantitative energy budgets are High School work.

relationships: A table, graph, or diagram is chosen because it fits the data and the claim, not because it looks impressive.
Axes are labelled with quantities and units, and the source and date of the data are stated.
A representation shows what was measured; anything added beyond the data is labelled as such.
accepted_alternative_framings: Bar, line, and scatter forms are each correct for the data they suit; the choice is judged on fit.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting a graph with unlabelled axes and drawing a conclusion from it.
Extending a line beyond the data and treating the extension as measured.
Choosing a representation that hides the variation in the data.
topics.out_of_scope: Statistical graphics conventions and error bars are later work.

relationships: Iteration means testing, using the result to make a specific change, and testing again.
One change at a time lets the effect of that change be identified.
A failed test is the normal and useful input to the next iteration.
disqualifying_errors: Changing several things between tests and attributing the improvement to one.
Declaring a design improved without retesting against the criteria.
Treating a failed test as a reason to abandon rather than as evidence.
topics.out_of_scope: Design of experiments and statistical optimisation are later work.

relationships: A scientific argument connects a claim to evidence by explicit reasoning.
The strongest opposing case is stated and addressed, rather than left out.
An argument reaches only as far as its evidence, and it says where that limit falls.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting claim and evidence with no reasoning between them.
Omitting evidence that counts against the claim.
Making a claim broader than the evidence supports.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal argumentation schemes and peer review are later work.
